source.title: Measuring Representational Robustness of Neural Networks Through Shared Invariances
source.authors: Vedant Nanda; Till Speicher; Camila Kolling; John P. Dickerson; Krishna P. Gummadi; Adrian Weller

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares representation-similarity scores with a directional shared-invariance measure, and reports that scores change substantially with the measure and with how inputs are generated. This bears on V6's metric and input dependence, while testing shared invariance rather than convergence of pairwise distances directly.
record.gate_note: Rows cover reported STIR/CKA comparisons and the arbitrary-versus-adversarial IRI comparison, which bear on metric/input dependence. The paper's other results about shared invariance across layers, datasets, architectures, training methods, and model updates are not treated as direct tests of the claim's distance-geometry or cross-modal behavior.
record.test_reason: The study contrasts in-distribution CKA with STIR, which scores target-model similarity on inputs generated off-distribution by inverting a reference model. For vanilla models, the high CKA convergence (0.967 across seeds) drops sharply under these inputs (0.56–0.61) and nearly vanishes under adversarial inputs (~0.06–0.09). This bears on V6: measured convergence depends on measure and inputs. Shared invariance itself is a related but distinct construct, so the layer and architecture invariance trends go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that CKA overestimates shared invariance (e.g. for vanilla models across seeds), while their directional STIR measure captures it faithfully. They also find that shared invariance falls with layer depth, rises sharply with adversarial training, is higher among residual architectures, and differs across robust-training methods. They treat worst-case (adversarial-IRI) STIR as near zero and too pessimistic to be useful.
record.recipe_differences: The paper generates inputs that preserve a reference model's representation and then compares target representations with linear CKA; this differs from ordinary same-input representation-similarity comparisons. The study does not test model-size scaling or cross-modal paired-data alignment.
record.method_sensitivity: Scores vary with arbitrary versus adversarial IRI generation, the reference/target direction, and the selected representation-similarity measure (STIR versus CKA).

fits_no_version.finding: Shared invariance (STIR) between differently seeded same-architecture models declines in later layers for vanilla training, while CKA stays high. Adversarial training makes all layers share high invariance (Fig 2, 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Same-architecture networks from different seeds share invariances mainly in early layers, unless training explicitly imposes invariance.

fits_no_version.finding: Across architectures, ResNets share more invariance with each other. AT models share high invariance across architectures (Fig 4, 8), but different robust-training methods (AT, TRADES, MART) share only ~0.5 STIR (Fig 5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Convergence of invariances depends on training objective more than on architecture.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 162, 2022
record.problems: Experiments are on CIFAR10/CIFAR100 image classifiers and do not test model scale, capability trends, cross-modal alignment, or out-of-distribution inputs. The main comparison concerns shared invariance, not pairwise distance geometry.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying V6 table results were omitted. The paper also reports further layer, dataset, architecture, and training-method comparisons, but these measure shared invariance and do not directly test the claim's distance-geometry, scale, or cross-modal versions.

untested.parts: No model scale or capability trend; only small CIFAR classifiers.
No feature, unit or subspace overlap across seeds. Only shared invariance and CKA are measured.
No mapping, stitching or relative representations.
Nearest-neighbour or kNN settings; distribution shift other than inversion-generated inputs.
Plateau of cross-model alignment; causes such as shared data or objectives versus a common reality model.

missing.what: Penultimate-layer STIR vs CKA matrix across ResNet18/34 and VGG16/19, vanilla and AT. Vanilla cross-architecture CKA is 0.88–0.95 while STIR is 0.14–0.68; CKA is uniformly high for similarly trained models.
Layer-wise STIR vs CKA for two seeds of ResNet18/VGG16 (and ResNet34/VGG19). For vanilla models, STIR drops in later layers relative to CKA.
Layer-wise STIR vs CKA across CIFAR10/CIFAR100-trained models.

record.verdict_notes: The CKA comparator rows (r5,r10,r15,r17,r19,r21,r23,r25,r27) should serve as baselines for the STIR rows, not as standalone results. r21, r25 and r27 duplicate values already given for the same symmetric pair. The record's single blanket 'supports' label hid the AT case, where STIR matches CKA. The study is not an original source. Code is released and the paper is peer-reviewed (ICML 2022).

versions.untested_parts: Model size/capability scaling and alignment of pairwise distances between independently trained models.
Vision-language alignment on paired images and captions, and its relation to model quality.
Whether same-architecture models share features or subspaces; the study measures shared invariance, not feature or subspace overlap.
Mapping or stitching representations, relative representations, or alignment without paired data.
Recurrence of interpretable features or circuits across models.
Out-of-distribution inputs, nearest-neighbour settings, and whether distance-geometry convergence changes under those choices.
Whether distance alignment plateaus or whether shared data/objectives explain it rather than a common model of reality.

relation.reason: Its experiments directly compare conventional similarity with shared invariance under arbitrary and adversarial input inversions.

tranche.reason: The study provides results and arguments qualifying representational alignment inferred from ordinary CKA through interventions on model inputs.

source_check.notes: STIR compares a target model's representations of original and inverted inputs; ordinary CKA compares two models on common inputs. Table 1 uses 1000 CIFAR10 training samples averaged over five runs; the model after the conditioning bar is the reference.
